newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court raps Renault for Belgian closure.
newsitem.headline: French court raps Renault for Belgian closure.

text.p: A French court on Friday barred automaker Renault from closing the Vilvoorde plant in Belgium until it consulted its European works council.
The ruling by the court in the Paris suburb of Nanterre followed a similar judgment issued on Thursday by a Belgian labour court.

Both courts ruled that in announcing the closure on February 27, Renault violated rules requiring consultations with staff representatives. But the judgments do not bear on the actual decision to close the plant.
Renault said it would appeal both rulings.
Despite angry protests by Renault workers in France and Belgium, the company maintains it will shut down the plant by the end of July as part of a reorganisation of its European assembly operations.
The Belgian court ruling "does not change Renault's decision to stop ordering vehicles from Renault Industrie Belgique on July 31, 1997," it said in a statement.
In the French ruling, the court said Renault failed in its duty to inform the European works council before publicly announcing plans to close the plant, which employs 3,100 people.

The court said advance consultations were required as the decision concerned Renault's "strategic orientation and was a major change in a European subsidary that would have repercussions at the European level".
It barred Renault from pursuing, "even through subsidiaries, the closing procedure for the Vilvoorde plant until it has fulfilled its obligation to inform and consult its European works council."
Renault said it would comply with the rulings and undertake the consultations required by the courts.
The Communist-led CGT union and the more moderate CFDT hailed the French and Belgian judgments and vowed to press ahead with their struggle to keep the plant open.

"With these two rulings, we have a basis to relaunch labour action not just against the Vilvoorde plant closure but also against Renault's plans to reorganise its dealer network and cut jobs in France," CFDT representative Daniel Richter said.

Serge Depry, a CFTC union delegate on Renault's European works council, told reporters he hoped the management would not just go through the motions but open a dialogue with the unions, which want Renault to save jobs by reducing working hours.
The unions had called on Friday for work stoppages and protests at Renault's plants in France, Belgium and Spain.
In Brussels, Belgian police turned water cannons on some irate workers as an estimated 1,000 Renault employees marched in protest through the centre of the city.

Police acted after some workers threw stones, firecrackers and eggs at officers in riot gear and tried to break through a barbed wire barricade in front of the offices of the Flemish regional government.
A spokesman for the Flemish government told them there was little that Flanders, where the doomed plant is located, could do. There were no reports of serious injuries or arrests.
